content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Juice, Pear is a 100 % natural fruit juice specially formulated for children from 1 year old. It is made from selected ripe pears, contains no added sugar, preservatives or artificial colours. The juice is low‑temperature pasteurised to retain maximum vitamins and flavour.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pear is one of the first fruits introduced to a toddler’s diet because of its soft texture and mild taste.
Baby Toddler juice undergoes strict quality control and meets European standards for infant nutrition.
The packaging is BPA‑free and safe for young children.
Each 150 ml serving provides about 30 % of the daily vitamin C requirement for 1‑3‑year‑olds.
No added sugar – sweetness comes from the natural sugars of the pears.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Source of dietary fibre
items.content: Fibre helps regulate bowel movements in young children.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium contributes to fluid balance and heart function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Pear flavonoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Gentle on the stomach
items.content: Low acidity makes the juice easy to digest for toddlers.

items.title: Pear allergy
items.content: Some children may be allergic to pears; monitor for reactions when first introduced.

items.title: Not suitable for infants under 1 year
items.content: Due to choking risk and digestive considerations, the juice should be given after the first birthday.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Even natural sugars should be accounted for within the overall diet.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the bottle refrigerated and consume within 48 hours.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the juice chilled in small portions (150 ml). It can be enjoyed on its own or mixed into baby cereals, yogurt, or purees to add variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened packages in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 2 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Collards (leafy cabbage) are a leafy vegetable from the Brassicaceae family, closely related to kale. They have large, slightly bitter leaves, a nutrient‑dense profile, and are commonly cooked, including sautéed in oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards thrive in temperate climates and can tolerate light frosts.
The deep green color comes from high chlorophyll content.
Unlike spinach, collard leaves retain their texture during long cooking.
In the Southern United States they are traditionally cooked with smoked meat and spices.
Collard seeds can be ground into a mustard‑like powder.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Collards provide a high amount of vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and C
items.content: Beta‑carotene and vitamin C support immune function and vision.

items.title: Contains calcium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals help maintain normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Collards contain oxalates, which may increase kidney‑stone risk in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Like other cruciferous vegetables, excessive raw consumption can affect thyroid function.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to Brassica vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Collards are typically sautéed in a small amount of oil until tender, added to stews, soups, or salads. Raw leaves can be blended into smoothies, but a quick blanch reduces oxalate levels.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store collards in the refrigerator in a plastic bag or container with a bit of moisture. They stay fresh for 5‑7 days. For longer storage, blanch and freeze the leaves.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-an.title: Egg omelet with meat and tomatoes

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet prepared with added meat (commonly ham or chicken breast) and tomatoes, cooked in a modest amount of fat. The dish is rich in protein, B‑vitamins, vitamin C from the tomatoes, and healthy fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable sources of complete protein.
Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
Meat adds iron and zinc, nutrients important for immune function.
Traditionally the omelet is fried in butter, but plant oils can be used to lower saturated fat content.
The dish is popular worldwide, from the American “Western omelette” to the Spanish “tortilla” with meat additions.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat provide all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs are rich in B12, while meat supplies niacin and riboflavin, aiding energy metabolism.

items.title: Tomato antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes deliver vitamin C and lycopene, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: The cooking fat can be a source of monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats when using olive or sunflower oil.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Meat provides iron and zinc; eggs add phosphorus and selenium, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white proteins.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Using large amounts of butter can raise saturated fat levels, which may be undesirable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with hypercholesterolemia should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogenic bacteria; ensure meat is cooked thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet hot, cut into portions. It can be eaten on its own, placed in a sandwich, added to a salad, or served alongside vegetables. Optional toppings include fresh herbs, cheese, or spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best consumed within 2–3 hours at room temperature. For longer storage, cool quickly and keep in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-to.title: Egg omelet with meat, tomatoes, and dark‑green vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet or scrambled eggs enriched with meat, tomatoes and dark‑green vegetables (such as spinach, broccoli or kale) is a nutrient‑dense dish providing protein, healthy fats and a wide range of vitamins and minerals. Added fat enhances flavor and aids absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable complete protein sources.
Meat boosts iron and vitamin B12 content.
Tomatoes add lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that is better absorbed with fat.
Dark‑green vegetables are rich in vitamin K, folate and chlorophyll.
Added fat (oil or butter) improves taste and helps absorb vitamins A, D, E and K.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and meat supply all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Vitamin A from eggs and tomatoes, together with vitamin C from tomatoes, supports normal immune function.

items.title: Bone health
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium from green vegetables help maintain strong bones.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and chlorophyll from greens protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: Fats and carbohydrates from the vegetables provide sustained satiety and energy.

items.title: Egg or meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs or certain types of meat.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Using processed meats with added salt can increase the dish’s sodium content.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improperly cooked eggs or meat can harbor salmonella or other bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs, a sprinkle of cheese or a drizzle of sauce. It can be eaten on its own, rolled in a wrap, or paired with toast as part of a breakfast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C. Do not leave raw eggs or meat at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit juice diet drink is a non‑alcoholic refreshing beverage made from concentrated fruit juices, sweetened with low‑calorie sweeteners, and fortified with vitamins. It is designed for people who watch their calorie intake but do not want to give up the taste of fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Diet fruit drinks often use stevia or sucralose instead of sugar.
Most brands add vitamin C to enhance flavor and antioxidant properties.
The drink may contain up to 30 % real fruit juice, the rest being water and flavorings.
Some versions are enriched with probiotics to support gut microbiota.
In many markets these drinks are sold in 0.5 L and 1 L bottles.

items.title: Low Calorie
items.content: A typical 250 ml serving contains only 30–50 kcal, making it suitable for a diet menu.

items.title: Vitamin Complex
items.content: Fortified with vitamin C, vitamin B6 and folate, the drink supports immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: With more than 90 % water content, it helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Fruit extracts and vitamin C provide antioxidant activity, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive Support
items.content: Some variants contain fruit pectin fibers that aid normal gastrointestinal function.

items.title: Fruit Allergy
items.content: People allergic to specific fruits (e.g., citrus) may experience reactions.

items.title: Artificial Sweeteners
items.content: Sensitivity to stevia or sucralose can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in some individuals.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may contribute to tooth enamel erosion with frequent consumption.

items.title: Sodium Content
items.content: Some brands add a small amount of salt for taste; those with hypertension should check the label.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve chilled, optionally with ice or fresh fruit slices. It works as a substitute for sugary sodas, a refreshing snack between meals, or a post‑workout beverage.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

pastry-made-with-bean-paste-and-salted-e.title: Pastry with Bean Paste and Salted Egg Yolk

content.title: About
content.content: Pastry with bean paste and salted egg yolk is a baked treat where a soft dough is filled with sweet bean paste and a savory salted egg yolk filling. Typically made with wheat flour dough, the combination of sweet bean and rich yolk creates a unique contrast of flavors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bean paste is a common sweet component in many Asian desserts, giving them a smooth texture and mild sweetness.
Salted egg yolk is a popular ingredient in Chinese and Thai pastries, adding umami and a buttery richness.
The pairing of sweet bean paste with salted yolk dates back to traditional street snacks of Southeast Asia.
The pastry dough is often leavened without yeast, relying on steam or short baking for a light, airy crumb.
Some regional versions enhance the filling with vanilla or coconut milk for extra aroma.

items.title: Rich plant protein source
items.content: Beans provide a notable amount of protein, important for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in the bean paste supports healthy digestion and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Both beans and egg yolk supply B1, B2, and B6 vitamins that are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are vital for immune function and oxygen transport in the body.

items.title: Moderate healthy fats
items.content: The salted yolk adds monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that can be heart‑friendly when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs should avoid this pastry, as the yolk can trigger reactions.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The salted yolk raises the salt level, so people monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The combination of dough, bean paste, and yolk makes the pastry relatively calorie‑dense; moderation is key for weight management.

items.title: Phytic acid presence
items.content: Beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The pastry can be enjoyed warm or at room temperature. It works well as a standalone dessert or paired with green tea or a light fruit salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate; it will stay fresh for about a week. Discard if any mold or off‑smell appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Apple pie is a classic dessert made of a pastry crust filled with sweetened apples, sugar, and spices. It is often served warm, sometimes accompanied by a scoop of ice cream or whipped cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Apple pie is considered a national dish in the United States and the United Kingdom.
The earliest recorded apple‑pie recipe appears in an English cookbook from the 14th century.
Cinnamon, nutmeg, and lemon juice are traditional additions to balance the flavor.
The United States hosts a “Best Apple Pie” contest during the annual Applefest.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Apples provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Apples contain vitamin C, which helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols in apples help combat free radicals.

items.title: Controlled sugar content
items.content: When homemade, the amount of added sugar can be adjusted, making the pie less sweet.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Pies often contain a lot of sugar, which can be problematic for people with diabetes.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The crust is usually made from wheat flour, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Apple pie is relatively calorie‑dense due to butter and sugar, so portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pie warm, cut into slices. It pairs well with a scoop of vanilla ice cream, whipped cream, or caramel sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a tightly sealed bag for up to 2 months; reheat in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Strawberry milk is a beverage made by blending milk with natural strawberry puree and a touch of sugar. It has a delicate pink hue, a sweet strawberry aroma, and a creamy taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Strawberry milk is often featured in children’s menus because it combines the nutrition of milk with the flavor of berries.
In some countries it is used as a base for smoothies and dessert sauces.
The strawberries used add vitamin C and antioxidants to the drink.
Traditionally it is prepared with whole cow’s milk, but plant‑based milks can also be used.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Milk provides calcium essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Vitamin C from strawberries
items.content: Strawberries contribute vitamin C, supporting immune function and iron absorption.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The milk base supplies complete protein important for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Strawberry flavonoids help combat free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The natural sweetness offers a quick source of energy, useful after physical activity.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consumption.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Allergy to milk proteins requires complete avoidance of the product.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweetened versions can raise blood glucose levels; moderation is advised.

items.title: Strawberry acidity
items.content: The acidity of strawberries may cause heartburn in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Strawberry milk can be enjoyed chilled as a refreshing drink, used in smoothies, added to cereals, oatmeal, or desserts. It is also popular as a milkshake topped with whipped cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store strawberry milk in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C in a sealed container for up to 3‑5 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or changes color.
